frameworks.name: Value Equation
frameworks.definition: A four-variable formula for product value: (Dream Outcome x Perceived Likelihood of Achievement) / (Time Delay x Effort and Sacrifice). Top variables create value; bottom variables destroy it.

frameworks.name: Four Types of Guarantees
frameworks.definition: A taxonomy of risk-reversal structures: (1) Unconditional, (2) Conditional, (3) Anti-Guarantee, (4) Implied/Performance-Based; can be stacked for maximum conversion.

frameworks.name: Trim and Stack
frameworks.definition: A value-engineering process: list every customer problem and solution, rank by customer-value and incremental cost to deliver, then keep only high-value/low-incremental-cost items.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that the Value Equation has four variables: Dream Outcome (how desirable is the promised result), Perceived Likelihood of Achievement (how believable is delivery), Time Delay (how fast does the buyer receive value after paying), and Effort and Sacrifice (what the buyer must start doing and stop doing). Increasing the top two and decreasing the bottom two produces a more valuable product.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Value is the ratio of desirability times believability over time cost times effort cost; manipulating any variable changes perceived value proportionally.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that most early-stage entrepreneurs focus almost exclusively on the top side of the Value Equation — making bigger promises and adding more testimonials — while the actual competitive moats in large businesses are built on the bottom side: reducing time-to-value and reducing buyer effort and sacrifice.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Reducing time delay and effort is operationally harder to replicate than adding marketing claims, creating durable competitive advantage.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that Dream Outcome (the first variable of the Value Equation) differentiates entire categories of products by price: business/investment outcomes tend to command higher prices than consumer outcomes such as weight loss, because buyers assign higher intrinsic value to financial gain than physical transformation.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: comparing B2B vs. B2C product categories
claims.mechanism: Buyer valuation of the promised outcome sets the ceiling for what the market will pay, independent of delivery mechanics.
bounded_by: Within the same dream outcome category, other variables determine relative price

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that Perceived Likelihood of Achievement (the second variable of the Value Equation) directly justifies higher pricing: a doctor with 10,000 liposuction procedures completed can charge more than a doctor with 1 procedure for the identical surgery, because buyers associate more experience with lower personal risk.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: same surgery, same outcome, same procedure time
claims.mechanism: Proof of prior success reduces the buyer's perceived risk of non-delivery, which increases their willingness to pay even when the actual delivery time is shorter for the experienced provider.

anchors.value: 1 procedure — lower price, lower perceived likelihood
10,000 procedures — higher price, higher perceived likelihood

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that Speed is one of the best all-time competitive advantages, because buyers value faster time-to-value not just a little more but dramatically more; the ability to deliver the same outcome in less time is itself a separate source of value independent of the outcome quality.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: The sooner a buyer receives a tangible result after paying, the lower the perceived risk of the transaction and the higher the experienced value.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that collapsing time-to-value to near-zero is a decisive competitive differentiator: a marketing agency that generates an inbound lead call within seconds of contract signing is radically more valuable than an agency delivering identical results at day 60, even when total outcome and cost are identical.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Immediate tangible output eliminates the buyer's anxiety window; value experienced immediately anchors commitment before doubt re-emerges.

numbers.axis: time from contract signing to first lead delivered

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that when full time-to-value cannot be compressed (e.g., writing a full book takes months), businesses should engineer an early tangible sub-result that proves the concept and breaks the buyer's limiting belief, even if that sub-result is smaller than the ultimate promised outcome.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: product delivery is inherently long-cycle (e.g., book publishing, real estate)
claims.mechanism: A completed sub-deliverable early in the journey serves as proof-of-concept, converting skepticism into commitment before the customer has experienced the full ROI.
bounded_by: Does not replace the full delivery; the early sub-result must be explicitly framed as a milestone, not the final product

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that the Effort and Sacrifice variable of the Value Equation has two components: what the buyer must start doing (new effort) and what the buyer must stop doing (foregone pleasures). Reducing both to zero maximizes perceived value of the offer.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Buyers resist purchasing when they anticipate new obligations or lost freedoms; eliminating those anticipated costs lowers the psychological action threshold.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that Netflix defeated Blockbuster because it lowered both the Time Delay and Effort and Sacrifice variables of the Value Equation to near zero — instant streaming eliminated the travel, selection, and return effort — while the Dream Outcome (watching movies) and Perceived Likelihood (certainty of watching) were equal between both services.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: same dream outcome and perceived likelihood for both competitors
claims.mechanism: Winning the bottom side of the Value Equation (time and effort reduction) produced decisive competitive advantage when the top side was equivalent across competitors.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that Amazon beat competitors by optimizing all four Value Equation variables simultaneously: one-click purchasing and next-day delivery reduced Effort and Time Delay to near-zero; review systems increased Perceived Likelihood of Achievement; and product selection matched any competitor's Dream Outcome.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: same products available from multiple sellers
claims.mechanism: Amazon's sustained investment in logistics (time) and UX (effort) plus reviews (perceived likelihood) created a compounding value advantage that pure product competition could not replicate.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that the four Value Equation variables directly map to marketing copy and headline structure: Dream Outcome = the promise, Perceived Likelihood = the number of people who achieved it, Time Delay = how long it took, Effort and Sacrifice = the stipulations or conditions. Claims built on all four variables are more compelling because they communicate value directly.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Persuasion and value are unified — buyers evaluate marketing claims using the same mental heuristics they use to evaluate purchase decisions, so claims matching the Value Equation structure feel more credible and actionable.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that the primary obstacle to purchase is not competition but inaction — buyers resist buying because the comfort of doing nothing is high. The seller's job is to lower the action threshold (reduce friction) until stepping over it becomes easy.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: The default alternative to buying is not a competitor but the status quo; risk and uncertainty sustain inaction even when the buyer is aware of the product.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that offering guarantees is a math equation: if an unconditional guarantee increases sales by 20% while increasing refunds from 1% to 5% (a 4-percentage-point increase), the net result is still a 15+ percentage-point gain in revenue, making the guarantee economically rational regardless of the emotional discomfort of higher refund rates.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: unconditional guarantee offered to all buyers
claims.mechanism: Guarantees shift risk from buyer to seller; because the seller has more information about delivery quality than the buyer, the seller can absorb that risk cheaply while unlocking conversion among risk-averse buyers.

numbers.axis: sales volume change vs. refund rate change from adding unconditional guarantee

bounded_by: Assumes seller can actually deliver the promised outcome at scale

claims.text: Alex Hormozi identifies four types of guarantees: (1) Unconditional — money back for any reason, the strongest type; (2) Conditional — money back if specific actions are taken and outcome is not achieved; (3) Anti-Guarantee — explicitly no refund, appropriate for knowledge transfers or highly effort-dependent outcomes; (4) Implied/Performance-Based — revenue share, profit share, or performance kickers where seller upside is tied to client success.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
bounded_by: Unconditional guarantee is strongest but only viable when refund economics are favorable
Anti-guarantee only works when the seller has a genuine proprietary asset or the outcome is demonstrably effort-dependent

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that stacking guarantees — combining a 30-day unconditional guarantee with a 90-day conditional guarantee — converts the initial sale into a trial, dramatically increasing close rates, and then makes the conditional guarantee's stipulations into the milestones proven to drive client success.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: B2B or B2C offers where client success milestones are known and measurable
claims.mechanism: The unconditional guarantee removes purchase resistance by eliminating perceived risk; the conditional guarantee's stipulations are reverse-engineered from successful client journeys, making compliance with those stipulations near-synonymous with achieving the promised outcome.

numbers.axis: guarantee duration and type in a stacked structure

anchors.value: 30-day unconditional — buyer can exit for any reason
90-day conditional — money back if 2-3 specific milestones are completed and outcome is not achieved

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that the conditional guarantee's stipulations should be reverse-engineered from the behavior of the customers who achieved the best results: identify the 2-3 minimum common actions those customers took, make those the guarantee conditions, and minimize the number of stipulations because each additional one weakens the guarantee's appeal.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: seller has sufficient customer success data to identify common success behaviors
claims.mechanism: Stipulations that mirror proven success behaviors are simultaneously effective as qualifying criteria (self-selecting compliant buyers) and confidence signals (each stipulation implies the seller is certain about the path to success).
bounded_by: More than 3 stipulations weakens guarantee appeal because it increases buyer-perceived complexity and effort

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that vague guarantee language (e.g., 'results guaranteed') suffers from banner blindness and means different things to different buyers; guarantees should spell out the exact outcome, the exact time period, the exact conditions, and the exact remedy in plain language — without necessarily using the word 'guarantee.'
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Specificity in guarantee language maps to specificity in the buyer's mental model of the outcome; vague guarantees reduce perceived credibility because the buyer cannot evaluate whether the promise is real.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that value engineering for a portfolio company begins with listing every micro-problem a customer encounters throughout their entire journey, writing the solution for each, then applying the Trim and Stack process: rank by customer value and incremental delivery cost, keep only high-value/low-incremental-cost solutions, and cut everything else.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: applicable to both physical product and service businesses
claims.mechanism: Concentrating delivery on items that are simultaneously high-value to the customer and low-incremental-cost to produce creates very high margin without sacrificing perceived value.

examples.text: Alex Hormozi contrasted a $50,000 liposuction surgery with a $5 weight-loss ebook, both promising the same dream outcome (weight loss). The surgery commands 10,000x the price not because the dream outcome differs, but because the surgery scores higher on all other Value Equation variables: higher perceived likelihood (surgical certainty), faster result (immediate physical change), and zero ongoing effort required from the buyer after recovery.

Alex Hormozi described two hypothetical marketing agencies offering identical lead-generation results. Agency A required the client to record ads four hours per week, attend three meetings per week, and wait 60 days for results. Agency B processed the credit card and immediately had an inbound lead calling within seconds, requiring zero ongoing client effort. Despite identical outcomes, Agency B is perceived as dramatically more valuable because it eliminates both Time Delay and Effort and Sacrifice.

Alex Hormozi gave the example of a book-publishing company in his Acquisition.com portfolio. Book publishing is inherently slow — a full book takes months. Rather than accept slow time-to-value, the company created a seven-day mini book bootcamp where clients could have a short published book live within a week. This broke the client's limiting belief that they couldn't write a book, proved the concept, and secured the buy-in to proceed with the full, revenue-generating book project.

Alex Hormozi illustrated a conditional guarantee structure for an internet marketing program: if the client purchased a domain, set up a website, and spent at least $100 in advertising within the program period, and did not achieve ROI within 90 days, they receive a full refund. The two or three stipulations — domain purchase, website setup, ad spend — are precisely the actions proven to drive client success in that program, so the guarantee is simultaneously generous and self-fulfilling for compliant clients.

Alex Hormozi shared a compliance-based guarantee example for coaching programs: require the client to write their daily plan in a Google Doc every morning and report what they actually did each evening for six weeks. Historical compliance rate for this activity is approximately 1-2%, meaning 98-99% of clients will never fulfill the condition. The guarantee appears generous but is nearly zero-cost in practice because almost no client completes the stipulation.

Alex Hormozi constructed a sample marketing claim using all four Value Equation variables: '70% of chiropractors we work with achieve over 100 patients in their first 30 days without having to make an ad.' Dream Outcome = 100+ patients. Perceived Likelihood = 70% achieve it. Time Delay = first 30 days. Effort and Sacrifice = without having to make an ad. This single sentence encodes all four variables and converts the Value Equation into usable copy.

practices.text: When designing a product or service, ask: 'How can I deliver the same outcome in half the time as everyone else?' — use this as the primary product differentiation question before investing in features or testimonials.

For any product with a long delivery cycle, engineer a tangible early sub-result that the buyer can hold in their hands within the first days or week, even if it is smaller than the ultimate promised outcome.
Spell out guarantee terms in plain language — exact outcome, exact time window, exact conditions, exact remedy — without using the generic word 'guarantee' if possible.
To design conditional guarantee stipulations, look at the 2-3 actions that clients who achieved the best results all had in common, and make those — and only those — the conditions of the guarantee.

When working to enhance the value of an existing product, build an exhaustive list of every micro-problem a customer could encounter across their entire journey, write a solution for each, then apply Trim and Stack: cut everything that is not simultaneously high customer-value and low incremental delivery cost.
Use the five value-enhancers when presenting any offer: scarcity, urgency, bonuses, guarantees, and naming that resonates with the target avatar.
